newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo central bank to seek stable dinar and low inflation. [CORRECTED 17:57 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Yugo central bank to seek stable dinar and low inflation. [CORRECTED 17:57 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects currency in headline from lev)

Tackling high inflationary expectations and growing corporate debt as well as maintaining currency stability will be the top policy goals of Yugoslavia's central bank, a senior bank official said on Wednesday.

"High inflatory expectations are the main problem of the country's financial system and are the worst to contend with," Djordje Djukic, member of the central bank board of governors said in an interview to Reuters.
The main priority of the bank's restrictive monetary policy in 1997 would be to maintain dinar stability and to ensure Yugoslavia's return to international financial institutions.
Djukic said there were "no quarantees that interest rates will fall unless the causes of inflation and inflationary expectations are curbed."
He said restrictive monetary policy could not be consistently applied without tackling the inter-company debt.
One solution would be to reschedule accumulated liabilities by using short-term securities.
"The central bank is preparing a proposal to convert commercial bank debt into short-term securities," Djukic said.
The internal debt stood at about 21 billion dinars ($4.2 billion) at the end of June, bringing it to the pre-1993 level before Yugoslavia suffered record hyperinflation of 60 percent a day.
According to Djukic, many firms did not intend to pay back their liabilites or would pay them only partly.
There was no conflict between the owners of capital and its users because "the users of capital (in Yugoslavia) are at the same time the biggest shareholders of the banks."
Djukic called for rigid financial discipline, saying "it must be strict enough to result in bankruptcies if necessary or the liquidation of some firms and banks."
He said that a vicious circle of high debts and high commercial bank lending rates, standing at 12-13 percent a month, harmed the efficiency of the monetary policy.
"This implies demands for correction of the exchange rate and writing off part of the outstanding credits," he added.
The dinar was last devalued by 70 percent in November 1995 with the set rate of 3.3 dinars to the German mark and has remained stable since.
Djukic said the effects of the monetary measures were very limited and called for effective fiscal and judicial policies.
"Debtors....are just waiting for a new wave of inflation and devaluation of the dinar to wipe off their debt as it happened in the last quarter of 1993," he said.
Analysts say the biggest debtors are large state monopolies whose directors or board members are at the same time ministers in the Socialist government.
Djukic accused government officials of lobbying to protect interests of different sectors and said their statements on the dinar rate destabilised the foreign exchange market.
"The government and central bank should suppress the causes leading to devaluation and not discuss whether or not to change the dinar rate," he said, and added:
"Who ever thakes such a decision (to change the dinar rate) must bear all the consequences."
